passage: At the school hobby club, trading card day was noisy. Eshaan, ten, laid out his spare cards and put a note next to his gold dragon card: "Ten cards only!" Sarika checked the club's trading list. "Dragons are worth three. Everyone knows that." "Not mine," Eshaan said. "Mine is special. I've had it since class three." Irawati offered four cards, then five. Eshaan shook his head. "You're trying to cheat me." By the end of the hour everyone had traded except Eshaan, who sat with his dragon and a sour face. "Nobody here knows what it's worth," he muttered.

qa.q: What does the club's trading list say dragons are worth?
qa.a: Dragons are worth three cards.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan think Irawati is trying to cheat him?
qa.a: Eshaan feels suspicious because the dragon is his and he has had it since class three, so it seems worth much more to him. A fair offer then feels like a trick.

qa.q: What could Eshaan ask himself before the next trading day?
qa.a: He could ask how many cards he would give to get that dragon from someone else; if the answer is three, that is probably a fair price.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel after offering five cards and being called a cheat?
qa.a: Irawati may feel hurt and confused, since five was already more than the list said.

grounding: Shows a boy demanding far more than his card is worth because it is his, and thinking others are cheating when they won't pay.

passage: I'm Gurleen, Kishore's elder sister, and I watched my brother try to sell his old cricket cards on our building's terrace. He had a stack of doubles. The other kids offered one rupee each, which is what they cost in the shop's mixed packets. Kishore asked for five. "These are from my collection," he said, as if that made them gold. Nobody paid. When the kids walked off, he told me they were all cheats who didn't understand value. Later I saw him counting the same cards in his room, very carefully. I'm not sure if he was upset or just stubborn.

qa.q: How much did the other kids offer for each card?
qa.a: The other kids offered one rupee each.

qa.q: Why did Kishore think the other kids were cheats?
qa.a: The cards felt valuable to him because they were his, so a fair price seemed like an insult rather than what buyers usually pay.

qa.q: How could Gurleen help her brother set a fair price next time?
qa.a: Gurleen could ask him how much he would pay for someone else's doubles, and suggest checking the shop price before asking.

qa.q: How might the kids who walked off see Kishore's price?
qa.a: They probably thought five rupees was silly for cards they could get from the shop for one, and didn't feel they were cheating anyone.

grounding: Shows a boy asking far more for his cards than buyers will pay because they are his, and calling the buyers cheats.

passage:
Monday: Chetan bought a shiny football card from the stationery shop for two rupees. It was just a card.
Wednesday: Leela wanted it for her album. "I'll give you three rupees." Chetan laughed. "Ten. It's mine now, and it's shiny." Leela said the shop had a whole box. "Then they're cheating people," Chetan said.
Saturday: The shop still had the box. Leela bought one for two rupees. Chetan watched her stick it in her album and felt strangely annoyed. His own card, still unsold, sat in his pocket, a little bent now.

qa.q: How much did Chetan pay for the football card?
qa.a: Chetan paid two rupees for it.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel strangely annoyed on Saturday?
qa.a: He had valued the card at ten because it was his, and seeing Leela get the same card for two showed his price was only in his head.

qa.q: What could Chetan try the next time someone wants to buy something of his?
qa.a: He could check what the same thing costs in the shop and ask himself whether he'd pay his own price, then offer a fair deal.

qa.q: How might Leela see the whole thing?
qa.a: Leela probably thought three rupees was generous, and found it simple to buy her own card from the shop instead.

grounding: Shows a boy pricing an ordinary card far above its worth once he owns it and blaming the shop, while a buyer gets the same card cheaply.

passage: Swati, you want to know why your Pappu Nana and I didn't talk for a week in 1966? Let your Neelam Dadi tell you. He was ten, I was eight, and he loved one cricket card: a bowler in mid-jump, with a torn corner. In our Meerut lane any card was worth two marbles, three at most. Pappu wanted ten. "It's worth more because it's mine," he said. None of the boys would pay. He came home furious. "They're all cheating me!" I said, "Bhaiya, would you give ten marbles for Bunty's card?" "Of course not, his is ordinary." I laughed, and he stopped talking to me. He never sold it. It's still in his tin box. He showed it to you last Diwali, remember?

qa.q: How many marbles did Pappu want for his card?
qa.a: Ten marbles.

qa.q: Why did Pappu think the other boys were cheating him?
qa.a: Pappu felt furious because the card felt very special as his, so offers of two or three marbles seemed unfair. He couldn't see that to them it was an ordinary card.

qa.q: What question did young Neelam ask, and how could it have helped Pappu?
qa.a: She asked if he would give ten marbles for Bunty's card. If he had thought about it, he might have seen that buyers and owners value the same thing very differently.

qa.q: How might the other boys in the lane have seen Pappu's price?
qa.a: They probably thought ten marbles was silly for a torn card and may have been annoyed at being called cheats.

grounding: A grandmother recalls her brother as a boy who demanded far more for his card because it was his, and thought the others were cheating.

passage: The school bus left in six minutes, and the card swap on the back benches was ending. Uday, eleven, held up his silver goalkeeper card. "Fifty rupees, or five cards." His classmate Harsha laughed. "Those are twenty. I'll give you twenty." "Twenty? It's mine. I've had it since Class 4." "It's the same card the stationery shop sells." The driver honked. Two more boys offered fifteen and twenty. "You're all cheating," Uday said, face hot. Harsha shrugged and got on the bus. Uday climbed on last, card in hand. Halfway home he thought: if it were Harsha's card, would I pay fifty? He didn't like the answer. He put the card in his pencil box and said nothing.

qa.q: How much did Harsha offer for the silver goalkeeper card?
qa.a: I'll give you twenty.

qa.q: Why did Uday feel the others were cheating him?
qa.a: He had owned the card since Class 4, so it felt worth much more to him. The buyers only saw an ordinary shop card, and he took their lower offers as unfair.

qa.q: What question did Uday ask himself on the bus, and how could it help him next time?
qa.a: Whether he would pay fifty if it were Harsha's card. Asking this before setting a price could help him see the gap between what owners and buyers think.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uday calling everyone cheats?
qa.a: Harsha probably thinks it's a bit unfair and silly, since twenty is the normal price, and just shrugs it off rather than arguing.

grounding: A boy rushing for the bus demands far more for his card because it is his, and accuses buyers of cheating when they won't pay.

passage:
Wednesday
Jasleen wanted my Golden Bowler card today. She offered three normal cards for it. THREE. I said ten or nothing. She said, "Nobody gives ten, Yogesh. It's not even that rare. Bunty has two." Yogesh

qa.a: Bunty was happy trading his card for three, which shows three was a fair offer.

passage: On the dusty ground behind the village school, Yusuf spun his old wooden top, the one with the chipped red stripe. Devika watched. "I'll give you my new paper kite for it," she said. It was a good kite, with a long tail. Yusuf snorted. "This top is worth your kite AND your marbles." "It's chipped!" "That's how you know it's lucky." Devika shook her head and went off to fly the kite with the other kids. Yusuf muttered to his cousin that she was trying to trick him. But when he asked Salim at the shop what a top like his cost, Salim said, "Five rupees new, beta." Yusuf spun it again, and it wobbled.

qa.q: What did Devika offer for the top?
qa.a: Her new paper kite, with a long tail.

qa.q: Why does Yusuf think his chipped top is worth so much?
qa.a: He feels proud and attached because it is his, so even the chip seems lucky and valuable, and a fair offer feels like a trick.

qa.q: What small step would help Yusuf judge a fair trade?
qa.a: Asking himself whether he would give a kite and marbles to buy a top like his, especially after hearing Salim's price.

qa.q: How might Devika feel walking off with her kite?
qa.a: Devika may feel a little annoyed that her fair offer was called a trick, but happy to fly the kite anyway.

grounding: A boy prices his own chipped top far above what others would give and thinks a fair offer is a trick.

passage: At the school swap fair in Manchester, Wei set out his old comics on a blanket with a big sign: £5 EACH. Omar flipped through them. "These are good. I'll give you £1 each for the space ones." Wei looked shocked. "They're worth way more. I've read those twenty times." "That's why the corners are bent," Omar said. The comic stall next door had the same issues for 50p. By lunch Wei had sold nothing, and he told his mum the other kids were trying to rip him off. She held up one of the space comics. "Would you pay five pounds for this, if it was someone else's?" Wei looked at the bent corner for a long time.

qa.q: What did the next-door stall charge for the same comics?
Why did Wei think the other kids were trying to rip him off?
qa.a: He felt upset and insulted because the comics were his and read twenty times, so they felt worth far more than buyers offered.

qa.q: Why is Wei's mum's question useful?
qa.a: It makes Wei look at the comic as a buyer would, which shows the gap between what an owner feels and what others will pay.

qa.q: How does Omar see the comics?
qa.a: Omar likes them but sees bent corners and cheaper copies next door, so £1 seems a reasonable offer.

grounding: A boy prices his own comics far above what buyers will pay and believes they are trying to rip him off.

passage: In the Class 5 classroom during the lunch break, children traded cricket cards. Santosh had a card of a fast bowler. It was common; everyone had three. But it was his. When Madhuri offered two cards for it, he laughed. "Two? It's worth at least six." "Six? I have that card at home already!" "Then why do you want it?" "For my brother. But not for six." Santosh crossed his arms. "You're trying to cheat me." Other children offered one or two cards. He refused them all. By the end of the break, he still had the card, and nobody would trade with him. "Everyone's a cheat," he muttered. Madhuri shrugged. "It's just a normal card, Santosh."

qa.q: How many cards did Madhuri offer for the fast bowler card?
qa.a: Two cards.

qa.q: Why did Santosh think the card was worth six?
qa.a: Because it was his, it felt more valuable to him, so fair offers felt like cheating, and he felt annoyed and suspicious.

qa.q: What could Santosh ask himself before naming a price?
qa.a: He could ask how many cards he'd give to get that card if he didn't own it, which shows what it's really worth.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see the card?
qa.a: Madhuri sees it as a common, normal card, so she finds Santosh's price silly.

grounding: It shows a child who demands more than his card is worth because it's his and thinks others are cheating when they won't pay.

passage:
Monday. Sumit brought his favourite football card to school. Vaibhav wanted it. "I'll give you three cards." Sumit said, "Ten." Vaibhav laughed and walked away.

Wednesday. Sumit asked other children. Nobody offered more than three. "You're all cheating," he said, angry. He put the card back in his bag.

Saturday. At the stationery shop, Sumit saw a packet of cards. Inside was the same football card. Sumit bought two packets and got the card twice. He stared at them. Then he went to Vaibhav's house. "You can have one for three cards," he said. Vaibhav grinned. "What changed?" Sumit shrugged, a little embarrassed. "Now I have two."

qa.q: How many cards did Vaibhav first offer?
qa.a: Three cards.

qa.q: Why did Sumit think the others were cheating?
qa.a: Because the card was his, he felt it was worth much more, so fair offers felt unfair and made him angry.

qa.q: What helped Sumit see the card's real value?
qa.a: Finding the same card in a shop packet showed it was common, so three cards suddenly seemed fair.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav seem to feel when Sumit comes back?
qa.a: Vaibhav seems amused and pleased, noticing Sumit's change of mind.

grounding: It shows a child who demands more than his card is worth because it's his and thinks others are cheating, over several days.

passage: Wasim, you think your friends are cheating you for your kite? Let me tell you about me when I was a boy of ten, in Lucknow. I had a kite with a red tail. It was ordinary, but it was mine. During Basant, my friend offered me his marbles for it. I said, "Twenty marbles." He said five. I said he was a cheat. I asked everyone. Nobody gave more than five. I was so angry I didn't fly it at all that day. That evening, my Abba asked, "Imran, if you had no kite, would you give twenty marbles for this one?" I thought. "No. Maybe five." He smiled. I felt silly. The next day, I traded it for five marbles and a ride on my friend's bicycle. It was a good deal.

qa.q: What did Imran's friend offer for the kite?
qa.a: Five marbles.

qa.q: Why did young Imran think his friend was cheating?
qa.a: The kite felt more valuable because it was his, so fair offers felt unfair and made him angry.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Imran's mind?
qa.a: Abba asked whether he'd pay twenty marbles if he had no kite, which helped him see its value as a buyer would.

qa.q: How might Imran's friend have felt when called a cheat?
qa.a: His friend might have felt hurt and annoyed, since five marbles was a fair offer.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, he demanded more than his kite was worth because it was his, until he asked what he'd pay as a buyer.

passage:
It was the last day of school before the summer holidays, and the bell was about to ring. Irfan wanted a new bat sticker, so he offered Chetan his shiny striker card.

"Five cards for it," Irfan said.

Chetan's eyes widened. "Five? They're one card each in the shop."

"But mine's special. I've had it since Class 3."

"It's the same card."

"Then you're cheating me!"

The bell rang. Chetan shrugged. "No deal, then." He ran for his bus.

Irfan stood in the corridor, holding the card. He felt cheated. But he also knew, deep down, that he wouldn't pay five cards for it either.

qa.q: How many cards did Irfan ask for his striker card?
qa.a: Five cards for it.

qa.q: Why did Irfan feel his card was worth five?
qa.a: Irfan felt proud of the card and cheated by the offer, because he had owned it since Class 3, so it seemed worth far more than to anyone else.

qa.q: What could Irfan ask himself before the next trade?
qa.a: Irfan could ask whether he would give five cards to buy the same card himself.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Irfan's offer?
qa.a: Chetan probably found it unfair and puzzling, since the same card costs one in the shop.

grounding: On the last school day, a child demands far more than a card is worth because it is his, and feels cheated when refused.

passage:
During Ganesh festival week, the colony kids spread their trading cards on the temple steps. Chinmay laid out his superhero cards.

Samir picked up one. "How many for this one?"

"That's my best one. Ten cards."

"Ten? Everyone knows it's worth two."

"No, it's worth ten. I've had it forever."

Samir put it back. "Then you're not being fair."

"You're the one being unfair!" Chinmay folded his arms.

Later, a younger boy offered Chinmay the same card for two. Chinmay grinned and said yes immediately.

Then he stopped. He had just bought the card for two, but he'd asked Samir for ten. His ears went red.

qa.q: Where did the colony kids spread their trading cards?
qa.a: On the temple steps.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay's ears go red at the end?
qa.a: Chinmay felt embarrassed, realising he had asked ten for his card but happily paid only two for the same one.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do next time he trades?
qa.a: Chinmay could ask himself what he would pay for the card if he didn't own it, and price it fairly.

qa.q: How might Samir feel when he hears Chinmay bought the same card for two?
qa.a: Samir might feel annoyed or amused, and maybe a bit vindicated that his price was fair.

grounding: During a festival, a child demands far more for his own card than he would pay, and realises the gap when he buys the same card.

passage: In the summer holidays, when it was too hot to go out, Santosh and I traded cricket cards on the cool floor of our building's stairwell. I had a shiny wicketkeeper card. I got it free inside a packet of biscuits, but once it was in my tin box it felt like treasure. Santosh offered two normal cards for it. I said ten. He laughed. "Ten? Nobody gives ten, Yusuf bhai." I was sure he was trying to cheat me because he wanted it so badly. I went upstairs angry and didn't come down till evening. The next week I saw the same card at the corner shop, inside packets anyone could buy. I still didn't trade it. But I stopped saying ten.

qa.q: What did Santosh offer for the shiny card?
qa.a: Santosh offered two normal cards for it.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf think Santosh was cheating?
qa.a: Once the card was in Yusuf's tin box it felt like treasure, so a fair offer seemed insultingly low and Yusuf felt angry and suspicious.

qa.q: What could Yusuf ask before setting a price next time?
qa.a: Yusuf could ask how many cards it would be fair to give if the card were Santosh's, which shows its value from the buyer's side.

qa.q: How did Santosh see Yusuf's price of ten?
qa.a: To Santosh it seemed silly and unfair, since it was an ordinary card anyone could get in a packet of biscuits 😅

grounding: Shows a child demanding far more than a card is worth because it is his own, and suspecting the buyer of cheating.
